front: What are the three main types of skeletal muscle fibre?
back: Slow oxidative (Type I) – slow twitch; Fast oxidative glycolytic (Type IIa) – fast twitch; Fast glycolytic (Type IIx) – fast twitch.

front: Where are the three types of muscle fibre found?
back: Within skeletal muscles; the proportion of each fibre type varies between individuals and is largely genetically determined.

front: Which muscle fibre type would an elite marathon runner predominantly have?
back: Slow oxidative (Type I) muscle fibres.

front: What are the characteristics of slow oxidative (Type I) muscle fibres?
back: -Slow contraction speed. -High resistance to fatigue. -High mitochondrial density. -High myoglobin content. -Dense capillary supply. -Well suited to aerobic energy production.

front: What sports are slow oxidative (Type I) muscle fibres best suited to?
back: Endurance events such as marathon running.

front: What are the characteristics of fast oxidative glycolytic (Type IIa) muscle fibres?
back: -Produce energy through both aerobic and anaerobic processes. -Moderate mitochondrial density. -Relatively resistant to fatigue. -Fast contraction speed. -Adaptable through training.

front: What are the characteristics of fast glycolytic (Type IIb) muscle fibres?
back: -Fast contraction speed. -Fatigue quickly. -Low mitochondrial density. -Low oxidative capacity. -Produce high levels of force and power for short-duration, high-intensity movements.

front: What sports are fast glycolytic (Type IIb) muscle fibres best suited to?
back: Explosive, high-intensity activities such as sprinting and high jump.

front: What are the effects of training on muscle fibres?
back: Muscle fibre type is largely genetically determined, but muscle fibres can increase in size through hypertrophy, resulting in greater strength and force production.

front: What does the autonomic nervous system do?
back: It regulates involuntary functions of internal organs and consists primarily of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.

front: How does the neuromuscular system work?
back: The nervous system and muscular system work together to control and produce movement.

front: What is the overall role of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems?
back: They regulate involuntary bodily functions, with the sympathetic nervous system preparing the body for activity and the parasympathetic nervous system returning the body towards its resting state.

front: What does the sympathetic nervous system do to the body?
back: It prepares the body for exercise through the "fight or flight" response.

front: What does the parasympathetic nervous system do to the body?
back: It promotes the "rest and digest" response, reducing activity and returning the body towards its resting state.

front: What does PNF stand for?
back: Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation.

front: What is PNF?
back: An advanced form of flexibility training that uses stretching and muscle contractions to increase range of movement.

front: What is a commonly used PNF technique?
back: CRAC: Contract – Relax – Antagonist – Contract.

front: What are proprioceptors?
back: Sensory receptors located in muscles, tendons and joints that detect changes in movement, position and tension.

front: What are the two proprioceptors important in PNF stretching?
back: Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs).

front: What do muscle spindles detect?
back: Changes in muscle length and the speed at which the muscle is being stretched.

front: What do Golgi tendon organs detect?
back: Changes in muscle tension.

front: Where are muscle spindles located?
back: Within skeletal muscles, running parallel to the muscle fibres.

front: What information do muscle spindles provide to the central nervous system (CNS)?
back: Information about the length of the muscle and the speed at which it is being stretched.

front: What happens after the CNS receives information from muscle spindles?
back: The CNS sends motor impulses back to the stretched muscle, causing it to contract and producing the stretch reflex.

front: What is the purpose of the stretch reflex?
back: To protect the muscle from excessive stretching by causing it to contract.

front: Where are Golgi tendon organs located?
back: Within tendons near the junction between the muscle and tendon.

front: What do Golgi tendon organs detect during PNF stretching?
back: Increased levels of tension within the muscle-tendon unit.

front: What happens during PNF when a muscle contracts isometrically?
back: Golgi tendon organs detect increased tension and send sensory information to the central nervous system, which leads to inhibition of the contracting muscle.

front: What is the result of the inhibitory response from the Golgi tendon organs?
back: The muscle relaxes through autogenic inhibition, allowing it to be stretched further and increasing range of movement.

front: What are muscle fibres grouped into?
back: Motor units.

front: What does a motor unit consist of?
back: A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it controls.

front: How many muscle fibre types are found within one motor unit?
back: One type; the muscle fibres within a motor unit are the same fibre type.

front: How does a muscle contraction occur within a motor unit?
back: A nerve impulse travels along the motor neuron to the muscle fibres, stimulating them to contract.

front: What do motor neurons transmit and where do they transmit them?
back: They transmit nerve impulses from the central nervous system to muscle fibres.

front: What are the physical features of a motor neuron?
back: A motor neuron has branches that connect to muscle fibres at neuromuscular junctions.

front: What are skeletal muscles made up of?
back: Many motor units of varying sizes.

front: What is found in a motor unit within a small muscle?
back: A motor neuron controlling a relatively small number of muscle fibres, allowing fine and precise movements.

front: What is found in a motor unit within a large muscle?
back: A motor neuron controlling a large number of muscle fibres, allowing greater force production.

front: What is the all-or-none law?
back: When a motor unit reaches its threshold, all the muscle fibres within that motor unit contract; if the threshold is not reached, none contract.

front: What is a motor unit unable to do according to the all-or-none law?
back: Partially contract; either all the muscle fibres within the motor unit contract or none do.

front: What is the threshold?
back: The minimum level of stimulation required to cause a motor unit to contract.

front: What happens if a nerve impulse reaches or exceeds the threshold?
back: All the muscle fibres within the motor unit contract.

front: What happens if a nerve impulse is below the threshold?
back: The motor unit does not contract.

front: What is wave summation?
back: An increase in the force of contraction caused by repeated stimulation of a muscle before it has fully relaxed.

front: What happens during the first stage of wave summation?
back: Each nerve impulse causes calcium ions to be released within the muscle fibre.

front: What happens if nerve impulses are repeated before the muscle has time to relax?
back: Calcium ions accumulate and the individual contractions combine, producing a stronger and more sustained contraction.

front: What is a tetanic contraction?
back: A smooth, sustained muscle contraction caused by rapid, repeated stimulation with insufficient time for the muscle to relax.

front: What is spatial summation?
back: The recruitment of additional motor units to increase the force of a muscle contraction.

front: How does spatial summation increase the force of contraction?
back: As greater force is required, more motor units are recruited, increasing the number of muscle fibres contracting.
